question: Which statement best describes Reducer function?
options: dispatch is the function useReducer returns for sending actions to the reducer. Calling dispatch(action) schedules a re-render during which React runs reducer(currentState, action) and uses the result as the next state. Importantly, dispatch has a stable identity across renders, so passing it down through props or Context — or listing it in effect dependency arrays — never causes unnecessary re-renders.

The reducer is a pure function with the signature (state, action) => newState that centralizes all your update logic in one place. Given the current state and an action describing what happened, it returns the next state — typically via a switch on action.type. It must be pure: no side effects, no mutation, and it should return the same state reference when nothing changes (the default case) so React can skip the re-render.

A reducer must return a brand-new state object rather than mutating the existing one. Mutating with methods like push or splice and returning the same reference means React's reference comparison sees no change and may skip the re-render. Always spread the previous state and override only what changed, or build a fresh array, so React reliably detects the update.

Actions are plain objects that describe an event, conventionally with a type string and an optional payload. The type drives the reducer's switch, while the payload carries any data the transition needs (like the text of a new todo or an id to remove). Keeping actions as serializable plain objects is what enables logging, time-travel debugging, and easy testing.

useReducer accepts an optional third argument, an init function, that computes the initial state from the second argument. React calls init only once on the first render, which avoids re-running an expensive initialization on every render. It also gives you a reusable function you can call again from a 'reset' action to rebuild the initial state.

question: Which statement best describes dispatch?
options: To share reducer state across the tree without prop drilling, wrap a useReducer in a Context provider and expose both state and dispatch. A common optimization is to split state and dispatch into two separate contexts, so components that only dispatch don't re-render when the state changes. This combination is effectively a lightweight, library-free Redux suitable for small-to-medium apps.

Reach for useReducer when the next state depends on the previous state, when several values change together, or when there are many distinct transitions. Stick with useState for simple, independent values. The reducer pays off by separating what happened (the action) from how state changes (the reducer), making complex update logic predictable and unit-testable in isolation.
